description: We are a team of curious and ambitious students passionate about space, astronomy, science, and technology. Our goal is to turn creative ideas into practical solutions using NASA's open data, scientific research, and innovative thinking. We value teamwork, problem-solving, and learning from each other, and we are ready to challenge ourselves to build a project that makes space science more accessible and engaging.
summary:
Finding uncharted objects like Planet X or faint asteroids comes down to one question: did anything move? NASA’s SPHEREx telescope photographs the entire sky in infrared every six months, creating massive datasets where moving objects leave faint trails.

We created Sky Blink, a fast web app that lets anyone visually explore this data. By aligning SPHEREx images taken months apart and blinking between them, objects that shifted immediately jump out. We also added comet tracking, difference views, and 96-channel infrared spectral plots.

Instead of downloading gigabytes of specialized files, anyone with a browser can now explore real NASA infrared data and help spot moving objects across the sky.
details:
What it does and how it works Sky Blink is a web app that lets anyone see what moved or changed in NASA’s SPHEREx infrared sky survey. Every six months, SPHEREx photographs the entire sky. When you pick a star, comet, or coordinate, Sky Blink pulls images of that spot taken months apart, lines them up, and lets you flip ("blink") between them. Stationary stars stay still, while moving stars, asteroids, or brightness changes jump right out. For fast comets like 3I/ATLAS, it stacks dozens of images on the moving object so faint targets become clear. It also plots the object's infrared spectrum across 96 wavelengths.

Benefits and intended impact Normally, reading SPHEREx data requires downloading large scientific FITS files and writing code. Sky Blink makes real NASA data instant and visual in any browser. Our goal is to help students, amateur astronomers, and researchers explore the infrared sky and join the search for moving objects, brown dwarfs, and distant worlds like Planet X.

Tools, coding languages, and software used We built the backend in Python using FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, and Astropy, connecting directly to NASA’s IRSA archive, JPL Horizons, and SIMBAD. The frontend is built with HTML5, CSS3, and vanilla JavaScript, using HTML5 Canvas for real-time image processing. We deployed the project on Vercel and Render.

How it is creative and factors our team considered Instead of just showing static pictures, we modernized the 1930 blink comparator used to discover Pluto, starting with an interactive scroll story of Barnard’s Star. Our team focused on three main factors: matching infrared wavelengths for fair comparisons, cleaning up bad detector pixels so sensor noise isn't mistaken for a discovery, and keeping the site fast and easy to use on mobile phones.
